paragraphs.text: [?] Solomon [?]. The Proverbs of Solomon son of David. The Saviour too is called “Son of David.” He, our peaceable Saviour, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, reigned in Israel. That is why, as he was completing the dispensation on behalf of humankind, the inscription over him read: “This is the King of the Jews.” The Jews are Israel, over whom [?] the Saviour reigns as over those who see clearly, if they are truly Israel. For not all who are the seed of Abraham are therefore also his children, since they do not do the works of
To know wisdom and instruction. Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human matters, a compre-

-hension. According to some, however, it is a breath of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; for nothing dark falls into it. For it is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. Whoever [knows] the works of wisdom knows these things, that is, the reflection of the eternal, the spotless mirror of God's working, and the image of his goodness. And this is nothing other than to know the Son of God's love, and Christ as wisdom. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. And this is revealed not by flesh and blood but by the heavenly Father. He also knows wisdom who has knowledge of the divine oracles: those of the Law and the Prophets, and of the Gospels and the Apostles. He lays his foundation on the rock, that is, on faith in Christ, so as to withstand rains and winds and blasts, that is, temptations arising from any quarter. If Luke says that he praised the steward of unrighteousness, he used the word “praise” loosely, applying it to the man's shrewdness and his sharpness of mind. This seems to be indicated also in “Now the serpent was the most prudent of all the beasts,” in the sense in which it is also said, “Be prudent as the serpent,” that is, not unacquainted with the serpent's villainies. To understand a parable and a dark saying, the sayings of the wise and riddles. Let us consider how these differ from one another. And first let us see what a parable is, starting from what the Gospels give us. For others too used the word “parable,” and so did Matthew, thus: “On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea, and the whole crowd stood on the shore, and he told them many things in parables: Behold, the sower went out to sow.” A parable, then, is a narrative told as of something that happened, which did not happen according to the letter but could have happened, and which figuratively indicates realities by transposing what is said in the parable. For “The sower went out” did not happen according to the wording, in the way we say the events of history happened; yet it could have happened according to the letter: “Behold, the sower went out,” and so on. I, however, think that when Jesus spoke in parables to those outside, to whom, because they were outside, it had not been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, he had gone out of the house, as Matthew recorded. Nor did Matthew write without cause and reason: “On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea.” For toward those who could not enter the house but were outside it, it was fitting that he should go out of it. That Matthew had something like this in mind in the passage will be clear to anyone who has observed what follows. For, it says, “Leaving the crowds, he went into his house,” and he reveals the meaning of the parable to the disciples. Observe in these words how Jesus speaks to the crowds in para-

-bles, and without a parable says nothing to them; and he does this to this day, for the crowds cannot take in the interpretation of parables. Note also how very intelligently “Leaving the crowds, he went into his house” has been written. It was not possible for the crowds to come in with him, but only for those who stood apart from the crowds, who were his disciples and could have the boldness to enter the house of Jesus. There, not as those who are outside but as those who have become able to be inside, they come to the teacher and ask to learn the inner meaning of the parables. And since they were able to follow him as he went into the house, he therefore answered their “Explain the parable to us” with what he said. Jesus not only goes out of his house, so that, having come outside, he might speak the parables to those outside, but he also sits by the sea, hinting that the crowds and those outside are not far from the waves of the sea and its salt water. Observe that great crowds gathered to Jesus when he had gone out of the house and was sitting by the sea. But it is no longer great crowds; rather the few who travel the narrow and afflicted way, and who find the way that leads to life, come in to him into the house as disciples. Examining, then, as far as I can, with reasoning befitting the Gospel, the intention of Jesus, who got into the boat and spoke in parables to the whole crowd on the shore, I say: perhaps the Word, for the crowds, neither having taken a stand nor standing, but being on the water of the sea, speaks while carried on that which, so far as possible, is able to stand upon water, namely what is called a boat. Do not be surprised if such thoughts have been expressed rather elegantly, so that the outsider and the crowd might not suppose that any meaning is hidden and stored up in the Gospel's arrangement, with dense subtlety; for this was the work of the grace that dispenses the word of God. I also try to hear more deeply both “The disciples came and said to him, Why do you speak to them in parables?” and “Leaving the crowds, he came into his house, and his disciples came to him saying, Explain the parable to us.” For the crowds, whenever they hear a parable, do not even notice that it needs explanation. But the disciples, observing that he speaks to the crowds in parables because they are outside, follow Jesus when he leaves the crowds; and seeing that they cannot learn the meaning of the parables anywhere except by entering the house of Jesus, they go in to him, and coming to him they say, “Explain the parable to us,” the one they wish to learn about. Such, then, is the parable. Next comes the dark saying. There are in the Scriptures some things said so deliberately obscurely that one could not grasp even a little in them without much and great examination, for they are confused both in phrasing and in thought

and in the arrangement of the words. This, I think, is what the book calls a dark saying. As an example of such things I shall set out from the Psalms what is said in Psalm 31: “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old,” and what follows. In plain terms, here the meaning can be understood according to the letter, as we shall show; but with a dark saying not even this is possible, as with this passage in Isaiah: “Woe to the land of the wings of ships, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends hostages by sea and letters of papyrus upon the water.” To clarify and understand each of these, illuminating its obscurity by exposition, is not for the present occasion, lest we make many untimely digressions. It is enough to clarify only the saying from the psalm, roughly thus: As long as I was crying out, praising God and speaking of God all day long, no part of me grew old, but rather I was renewed. But when I grew idle in speaking of divine things and kept silent, then old age entered even into my bones, into what seemed strongest in me. And upon this followed your hand becoming heavy upon me night and day; and therefore your hand, weighing upon me, turned from its former care for me to my wretchedness. And I deserved to suffer this, since a thorn was fixed in me when I was held fast by cares, or by wealth and the pleasures of life. That the Prophet had something of this kind in mind here is clear from what follows: “I acknowledged my sin,” and so on. After this we may see what the sayings of the wise are; then what riddles are; and the sayings of which wise men the wise man hears, and by hearing them becomes wiser himself. Are they only those of the men who are wise according to God and his truth, or not only these but also those whom God catches in their craftiness? For Scripture has called these wise too. For why should the man spoken of understand the sayings of the blessed wise, yet not be able to understand the words of the other wise men as well, but have a mind inferior to the mind of the wise of this world, unable to follow what they say? Perhaps, just as it is the work of the eye to see not only things that are well ordered but also those that are otherwise, or as the art concerned requires, so it is the work of the mind to contemplate both the conceptions that hit the mark and those that do not. Then he himself will not be caught by the plausibility of falsehoods, and he will rescue those who have been caught, if he understands the sayings of the other wise men too, where they use sophistry, how they reason fallaciously, how the sophism is resolved and the fallacy refuted. For in this way God also threatens through his own wise men that he will set aside the wisdom of the wise, which deserves to perish because of its falsehood, and the deceptive understanding of those who are not prudent according to him; and so through his own wise men he will catch the wise of this age in their craftiness. [?] The disciples of the Lord, if they had not understood the sayings of the

worldly wise, how could they have waged war for the pulling down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing exalted against the knowledge of God? And how could anyone perfectly keep what Peter says, “Always be ready to make a defence to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you,” without being fully prepared in speech, so as to be ready to make a defence for the hope that is in him to every Greek and every barbarian, to every wise man and every fool, by understanding the sayings of the wise, accusing some, overturning others, and establishing and demonstrating still others? Do not be surprised if nowadays one who is truly wise according to God is not found; for most of the special gifts have died out, so that they are found either not at all or rarely. It remains to explain what riddles are. I think a riddle is a narrative about things as though they had happened, which did not happen and cannot happen, but which signify something secret in a hidden way. Take as an example the passage in Judges: “The trees went forth to anoint a king over themselves.” Who the three fruit-bearing trees are, the fig, the vine and the olive, which did not wish to reign over trees unworthy of their reign; and who the thorny bramble is, which lets fire out of itself to devour the cedars of Lebanon, it is for the wise man to see, referring the former to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the bramble to the Adversary. There is also such a riddle in Kingdoms: “The thistle in Lebanon sent to the cedar in Lebanon, saying, Give your daughter to my son as wife,” and what follows. You may also find riddles in the prophets, as in Ezekiel: “The great eagle, great-winged, long in extent, full of talons,” and what follows. This is as much as we have been able to take in for the present on the subject at hand. These, then, were parable and dark saying, the sayings of the wise and riddles. A parable is a narrative told as though about something that happened, which did not happen according to the letter but could have happened, and which figuratively indicates hidden things, as in “The sower went out to sow”; for this did not happen according to the wording, even if it is referred to other things. How then does “I will open my mouth in parables” fit this? For what he added did happen: “In the sight of their fathers he did wonders.” And according to the letter he split the sea and led them through. All these things happened, even if, taken in the manner of the Gospel parables, they are symbols of the things to which they were referred. But someone else will say that “I will open my mouth in parables” refers not to the events of the Exodus but to the parables in the Gospel, Christ saying in the prophet, “Attend, my people, to my law,” and what follows. A crown of graces. Or the circle of the virtues, because they are bound to one another.

and a golden chain about your neck. By the golden chain he means the radiance and circular brightness of the divine oracles; and by the neck he means the mind. Let us take his memory away from the earth. These words might also be ascribed to those who said, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, so that the [?] may be ours

Cast in your lot with us. Abandon that way of life and be with us; keep the Sabbath with us, keep the feast of unleavened bread with us, and the other observances of the law. For they themselves, sharing in [?]. For God is the giver of good things, but we are the cause of evils, that is [?]. You might also apply these words to the Jews who shared in the blood of the prophets and of Christ himself. These are the ways of all who accomplish lawless deeds. By “accomplish” I think is meant not simply doing something, but filling up the measure of their fathers and being liable for all the blood from Abel to Zechariah. Wisdom is sung in the ways out. While she is silent within the wise man she is not sung; but when she finds a way out, she is sung. For it shall be, when [you call upon] me. For we call upon Wisdom as Lord, since she is Christ. So whoever calls upon Christ, if he understands who he is, calls upon wisdom, understanding, sanctification, righteousness and every virtue, if not with his lips, then with his deeds. But let us not become such that we call upon him and he does not hearken to us. If, receiving the saying of my commandment, you hide it within yourself. A person hides it when he keeps it not for vainglory but taking pains to go unnoticed. Then you will understand the fear of the Lord. See after how many things we shall understand the fear of the Lord; for it too is obscure, as is clear from simpler cases. For one can see some people fearing the Lord where they should not, and not fearing him where they should. And give your voice to understanding. Each person gives his voice to something: perhaps to anger, uttering what belongs to it, or to grief, or to fornication. But the blessed man dedicates his whole voice to the Lord, so that whatever he speaks may be wisdom. As another seeks silver, so you should seek wisdom, becoming as it were a lover of money in this. Let not evil counsel overtake you. Those who are strangers to the Church promise one thing at the beginning and another at the end. At first they turn people away from idolatry and bring them to the Creator; then, changing course, they reject the Old Scripture, contra-

-dicting the elementary teaching of youth. But among the teachers of the Church the end agrees with the first elements. CHAPTER 3. And let your heart keep my words. After the commands and prohibitions of the law of God, the words of the wisdom of God proclaim the unerring knowledge of the things that are. Of this kind is also “Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” For whoever keeps the laws will take up wisdom. For it says, “Sow righteousness for yourselves; gather the vintage for the fruit of life.” Then, after the practical, it adds: “Light for yourselves the light of knowledge.” Provide what is good in the sight of the Lord and of men. If you do whatever you do in wisdom, you will be a son of God, as it is said, “You made all things in wisdom.” Honour the Lord from your just labours. Divine Scripture usually uses the word “honour” for giving. For it says, “Honour widows who are truly widows,” instead of “Share with them,” so as not to humble the widow by saying “alms.” And the Saviour says, “It is written in the law: Honour your father and your mother,” and so on. He said “from just labours” so that it might not come from robbery and greed. And let no one hesitate to give; for he will have no excuse after the widow in the holy Gospel who cast in her whole living and was justified, not above those who gave from robbery, but above those who gave from their abundance. Everything is a gift to God: the works of temperance and of the other virtues. For one must give firstfruits of all produce to the Church and to the poor; and on rising from sleep one must give God prayer as firstfruits; and it is fitting to give psalms as the firstfruits of one's words. For thus it will be said to you: “And blessed are your storehouses and what you leave over”; and he means those of the soul. God founded the earth by wisdom. But the faithful soul too is earth, bearing fruit a hundredfold. It becomes wise from the richness that is wisdom, God founding it upon that richness. For he establishes in it the first introduction to teaching, making it firm through wisdom; and as it continually advances, he makes it a heaven, a most pure creation, a dwelling of angels and intellectual beings. Receiving a perception of what is, and understanding things in their precision, it begins to distinguish and dissect them.

[?] [A precious soul] hunted by a woman: the soul is precious by nature, for it is not earthly by nature. Or: since the mind of the courageous and their soul are precious, she nevertheless hunts these too.

I was the one in whom she rejoiced. “I was,” said of God, does not signify time; for it is temporal when it signifies something subject to time, as in “I was in the marketplace.” But if she was with God, as befits the one without beginning, eternal

She enriches. If everyone blessed by the Lord is rich, and those who walk in the law of the Lord are blessed by the Lord, and the prophets walked in the law of the Lord, then they were rich. A fool does evil in laughter. When he does evil he is pleased and rejoices. But wisdom bears prudence for a man, that is, practical virtue. He who does not deal kindly with his own house will inherit the winds. Our God is the house in which we move and have our being. So whoever does not walk in God's commandments will be a co-heir with the opposing powers. From the fruit of righteousness grows a tree of life. The fruit of righteousness is the goal of virtue. A person has as many trees of life as he has fruits of righteousness. This tree of life is the one planted in the middle of paradise, which Adam was prevented from touching after his sin, having lost the seeds of righteousness from which the tree of life grows.
He will be his own friend. Origen makes no mention of this verse at all, but it was found in some copies; for it is neither in the Seventy nor in the others

Three things are impossible for me to understand. A theorem is impossible for someone just being introduced to scientific understanding; and it is impossible for a human being to contemplate and understand what is beyond the human, such as the cure for cancer, even though angels know it; and what in no way exists and cannot come to be, such as three being four, is impossible for anyone to conceive. So it seems to have been said about things that do not exist. For since an eagle leaves no tracks when it flies through the air, analogously to those left

[?] footprints left in the sandy ground [?], it is impossible to make them out. So too with the serpent: on yielding ground its ways can be made out, but on rock they cannot. And the paths of a ship crossing the sea. Perhaps in these words we should take the ship to mean Jesus and his disciples, though sometimes the disciples alone. That ship does not keep crossing the open sea, for at once, by divine power, the boat reached the land they were heading for. But a ship that does not carry Jesus crosses the open sea, and does so continually, tossed about by contrary winds. And since the affairs of this life are vanity, with people always out at sea and none of them making progress toward eternal life, their paths cannot be made out. So of the glorious kings or rulers of the earth, no work foreign to godliness is left behind after death, for their glory has been extinguished. Nor, it says, are the ways of a man in his youth recognized, a man inflamed with desires, because his habits are so unstable; and likewise the ways of the adulterous woman, because of her shamelessness. Or this is the Church of the Gentiles, who, after washing herself clean through baptism, says she has done nothing wrong. But the righteous man is not “in his youth,” since, made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled long years. Such too is every adulterous woman who has estranged herself from her bridegroom, and every soul that has left her husband and goes after her lovers. And it marches in good order at one command. The locust too is praised for its good order, because it obeys the command of the Word of God. The Church is something like this. Because she is despised by people, she is compared to a locust as regards her life on earth. But because she gathers with Jesus and does not scatter, and puts on the whole armor of God so that she can stand against the schemes of the devil, she encamps in good order at a single command. She has no king as far as Pharaoh is concerned, but not as far as God is concerned, and the labors of the Egyptians are handed over to her. Perhaps the locust is kingless because we had no king before the kingdom of Christ. For locusts have no leader as bees do; each one leads itself. These are the people who by their own choice are relieved of earthly things and walk an ordered life. Or the locusts are those who want to fly by contemplation but cannot, and rise only a little way above the earth. But if they take up the practical life, they will be brought into one practical rank. And a he-goat leading the flock. The third is the he-goat, found only in the Septuagint, which leads the flock, makes it grow and multiply, and guides it to the pastures on the heights. For no other herd of animals climbs the heights like this. Such is the one who leads for Christ [?], bringing those in the flock up to the heights. Alternatively, the he-goat prefigures Christ, who was offered for sin. Since he is on high, the whole multitude of the godly follows him.
